coverage.assessment: The Beethoven premise from 007 survives, as do the clerk's map and the Stelvio mechanism. Two revision cuts loosen links: the women's moral sense no longer resolves the dilemma (F1), and 'Even the greatest of men' has lost its 'for' clause (F5). 'Suddenly' in para 6 now has no preceding state (F2).

Thun, Milan, Stelvio, Mals, Dresden, Florence, Rome, Naples and Palermo remain correctly sequenced. Cutting the Jager officers' courtesy and the father's Congress seat leaves no confusion; 009 supplies 'Member of Congress'.
The hypothetical 'Sir, I am a tourist!' is intact. Browning's report and Garibaldi's 'few words of talk' stay summarized, as they are in the source. No attribution problems.

The 'third failure' remains speculative. The Autobiography remark is cut, an authorized option, so no unconditional claim appears. Seward support is kept without anticipating Lincoln. 'Perhaps it meant nothing' survives.

The revision strips several markers of the old narrator judging the young man: 'Of the Germany to come, he knew nothing' (F2), the later shame over the Courier letters (F3), the tourist disclaimer (F5), and the forward line about Garibaldi's class of mind (F7). There is no premature revelation.

The irony is preserved in the major set pieces. Some comic deflations are lost: the Browning slowness and guillotine consolation (F6), and the Frau Hofrathin's 'huge laughter', which the revision cut, leaving the social failure abstract. The anachronistic '1960' leap is also gone (first draft).
The causal-sequence premise of Rome is weakened (F4). The closing ledger loses its 'perhaps Paris served better' turn on accidental education (F8).
Ara Coeli/Gibbon, the gay sister, and the Palermo scene are intact at both endpoints. The King plant was removed under its optional allowance, and 022 introduces King coherently.

findings.claim: The revision deletes the sentence explaining that a woman's will 'ends by settling the moral'. It also deletes 'she wanted him much to be civilized'. 'Luckily for him' is the answer to the unanswerable question of when robbery and murder become virtue, and without these sentences it reads as a mere transition.
findings.counterevidence: 'Luckily for him' and the general law survive, so the woman-as-guide theme is still legible.

strengths: All eight verbatim passages survive exactly, including the typographic 'Why! Why!! Why!!!' and the glow-worm deflation.
The Stelvio barricade sentence, with even Mrs. Kuhn gasping and gun barrels lost in the flash of the snow, is preserved whole.
The Garibaldi sphinx paragraph keeps its triple conditional ('might be a Napoleon or a Spartacus…') and its hedged reading of his character.
The 'two great experiments… failure of a third' sentence stays speculative, and the chronology (Thun, Florence, May, June) is accurate.
summary: The revision is coherent and keeps every verbatim line, the planned chronology, and all three required dependencies. It runs about 2,700 words, under the 2,800 target. Its new cuts remove several hinge sentences rather than ornament: the women's-moral-sense law that makes 'Luckily for him' answer the moral dilemma, the 'floundering between worlds' frame, the retrospective shame over the Courier letters, Rome's premise for 'young men… taking for granted that everything had a cause', and the tourist disclaimer at Ara Coeli. Each loss is small, but together they thin the old-man/young-man layering and the logic linking episodes. Older first-draft losses (Browning irony, the Paris 'perhaps') are tradeoffs. There are no must-fix blockers.
